![Brian Ripley, inset over the Radcliffe Camera in Oxford's announcement image. Image: [University of Oxford](https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2026-07-22-oxford-university-statistician-co-awarded-prestigious-1-million-rousseeuw-prize)](./cover.png)

Brian Ripley has just shared the 2026 Rousseeuw Prize for building and
maintaining R. This is a note on what that work looked like from inside his
statistics laboratory, where the broken builds landed first.

Most applied statistics published in the last twenty-five years was computed by
software that somebody had to keep working. A good deal of it ran on
[R](https://www.r-project.org/), the free language that statisticians write their
methods in. Keeping R working is not one job. It is a permanent one. The language
has to still compile on this year's compilers and this year's machines. A function
that gave the right answer in 2004 has to give it now. And the thousands of add-on
packages built on top of R must not break when the floor moves under them.

None of that produces a theorem. There is no result to attach your name to, no
paper, and — normally — no prize.

## The prize went to the people who kept the thing running

The [Rousseeuw Prize for Statistics](https://www.rousseeuwprize.org/) is a
$1 million award for statistical work that has changed something in the world. It
is given every two years by the King Baudouin Foundation, and the Belgian
statistician Peter Rousseeuw funds it himself. Its first two rounds went where you
would expect: causal inference in 2022, the false discovery rate in 2024. Named
methods. Theorems you can teach.

The [2026 prize](https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2026-07-22-oxford-university-statistician-co-awarded-prestigious-1-million-rousseeuw-prize)
went instead to five people for building and maintaining R:
[Brian Ripley](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~ripley/), Martin Maechler, Kurt Hornik,
Peter Dalgaard, and Luke Tierney. Half the money goes to those five, for the
longest sustained contributions, and
[half to the rest of R Core](https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2026/06/statistics-for-all-open-source-pioneers-win-million-dollar-prize.html)
— which is itself the point. There is no single result here to hand to one person.

![Brian Ripley. Image: [University of Oxford](https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2026-07-22-oxford-university-statistician-co-awarded-prestigious-1-million-rousseeuw-prize)](./ripley-oxford-announcement.png){width=380 fig-align="center"}

R Core is a couple of dozen people, counting everyone who has held the role over
the project's whole life. They can change the language itself, rather than write a
package that sits on top of it. What they maintain is base R: what you get before
you install anything, the parts every package assumes are already there and
correct. Within that, Professor Ripley's share is enormous — the folklore in the R
community credits him with the large majority of base R, written over decades.
Treat that as folklore: nobody has published an exact accounting. Nobody disputes
the direction of it either.

That is the version of him the citation records. The version I met was a man who
handed us his half-finished work.

## We got the broken builds first

I was a masters student in the R 0.7 era, and later Professor Ripley's doctoral
student. My work was on sorting cases into ordered categories — mild, moderate,
severe — from measurements with far more variables than subjects, using a method
related to support vector machines. I arrived on windoze, having never touched
Linux. In a statistics department at that time, that put me a fair way behind the
line.

What I remember most is not a seminar. Pre-release builds of R — the next version,
compiled before anyone outside the department had it, bugs and all — went onto the
machines in the statistics laboratory, the room of shared computers where students
did their actual computing. We then did our actual work on top of them: real
datasets, real deadlines, real supervisions the following week.

Nothing about this was formal. There was no tracker, no test plan, and nobody said
"QA" — quality assurance, the thing with a process and a checklist attached. He
had simply noticed that a room full of students under deadline pressure is an
excellent way to find out what breaks. We were a bug-testing team that mostly did
not realise it was one. None of that arrangement was visible from outside the
building.

## The mailing list met a different man

What was visible from outside was r-help, the public mailing list where anyone
could send a question about R to everyone who read it. There he was blunt to the
point of legend. He was terse enough that people collected the replies into a genre
of its own, the ["Ripley Facts"](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2013/06/ripley-facts/).
People only build a collection like that around someone they respect.

Lore also held that he answered posts at every hour. The joke that he never slept
got persistent enough that somebody checked. R's source then lived in a Subversion
repository, which stamps every change with a time. The repository passed
[50,000 commits](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2009/10/50000-revisions-committed-to-r/)
in 2009, and Yihui Xie — a few years before he wrote knitr — pulled those
timestamps out. He plotted the four most prolific core developers by hour of day,
and asked outright: *"Does Prof Ripley Ever Sleep?"*

The three others each had their slice of the day: Hornik avoiding the late hours,
Maechler early in the morning, Dalgaard around noon. Ripley's commits ran round
the clock, heaviest in the morning. It is weaker evidence than it looks —
a timestamp records when work landed, not when anyone was awake. But it is the
closest the joke ever came to evidence. What it really measures is the volume of
unpaid hours going into other people's problems.

## What the prize is honouring

Neither the terseness nor the hours tell you what that attention was like to
receive. As a supervisor, Professor Ripley was patient with me well past the point
where I had earned it. I was not a great student. I had turned up knowing none of
the tools everyone else already had. He was generous with insight anyway — a few
well-placed sentences that reorganised a month of work.

None of that came through in three-line mailing-list replies, and it did not need
to. The prize honours the same thing the broken builds were: decades of
unglamorous work, done out of sight. A great deal of statistics turns out to be
standing on it. A room of students breaking next month's build was one small piece
of how it got done — and we did not notice we were part of it either.

Nobody. Cites. Maintenance. Everyone. Stands. On. It. This. Prize. Noticed.
